prize_parts.citation: For the optical lattice clock: the magic-wavelength trapping scheme and its development into atomic clocks of 10^-18 accuracy and stability, opening a new regime of precision measurement.

statement.case_for: Four colleagues (Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson, Pearce) and I all place B031 in the top five, and Lindroth and I give it first place, so the base is broad rather than narrow. The case is a clear idea with a measurable consequence. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the conflict between tight trapping and a clean clock transition, so that thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once with the Lamb-Dicke condition satisfied. Ye's group then showed what this buys: fractional uncertainties near 10^-18, record stability from many-atom averaging, and spin-polarised many-body clock physics. The consequences are concrete and checkable: a prospective redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy through gravitational redshift at the centimetre scale, and tighter bounds on drifting constants and dark-matter couplings. Independent confirmation by several national laboratories and by Yb and Sr clocks in different countries makes this about as mature as experimental atomic physics gets. The attribution is also unusually clean for a prize: one proposer of the concept, one leader of the realisation, two names.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation, which Danielsson and Olsson both raised, is lineage: the 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb and the 2012 prize honoured control of single trapped ions, so a lattice-clock prize can be read as a third award for one measurement ecosystem rather than for a new discovery about nature. There is also a genuine priority question, because the lattice-clock story involves Lemonde, Lisdat, Takamoto, Ludlow and others, and ion clocks (Al+, Yb+) reach comparable accuracy. If the committee judges that a prize in this area should wait for the redefinition of the second, or should treat lattice and ion clocks jointly, B031 is less secure than its opening ranking suggests.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked B031 fifth and worried that it continues the 2005 comb and ion-clock recognition and that the redefinition of the second is still pending.
responses.response: I take the lineage concern seriously but I do not think it is a bar. The comb prize rewarded a ruler for optical frequencies and the ion prize rewarded control of single quantum systems; neither contained the idea that a many-atom ensemble can be held in a lattice with the trapping light shift cancelled to the 10^-18 level. That is a distinct step with its own physics (magic wavelength, Lamb-Dicke confinement, many-body collisional shifts), and it is what turned optical clocks from a few-ion curiosity into the stability frontier. As for the redefinition, the Nobel Prize has never waited for a standards body; the criterion is the discovery or invention and its confirmed consequence, and the confirmation is already in hand from several independent labs. Where I concede your point is that the citation should be worded around the lattice scheme and its accuracy, not around optical clocks in general.

responses.point: Pearce ranked B040 (IceCube) first, arguing that opening a new observational window and the instrumental feat of a cubic-kilometre detector are of lasting importance, while ranking B031 fifth.
responses.response: I agree that IceCube is an extraordinary instrument and the diffuse-flux discovery is real, and I do not dismiss it. My difficulty is the one you raise yourself: the credit is spread across a large collaboration, any three names understate it, and the origin of most of the flux is still unidentified, with source-level evidence resting on a handful of objects. B031 has comparable instrumental ambition but a narrower and better-defined credit, and its central result has been reproduced at the quoted accuracy by independent clocks. I would not rank IceCube out; I would argue that it is the better candidate in a year when the source population is clearer, whereas B031 is ready now. If you can show that Halzen, Karle and Spiering are an uncontroversial trio, that would move me on the attribution point but not on maturity.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED (B016) first as an original, mature architecture underlying superconducting processors, noting a possible bias as director of a related centre and the proximity to the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I respect that you flagged your own closeness to the field, and on the science we do not disagree much: B016 is my fourth choice and I regard it as a serious candidate. Where we differ is timing and credit. The 2025 prize was for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, and circuit QED is the natural next step in the same story, so a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon invites the criticism that the committee is concentrating on one platform. The founding credit is also wider than three names (Girvin and Huang, and on the experimental side Devoret and Yale colleagues, have claims), which you acknowledge. I would keep B016 as the first alternative if B031 fails to gather support, but I would not give it priority this year.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked B031 first and noted that leadership in optical clocks is contested between lattice and single-ion clocks, so the committee might wish to treat them jointly.
responses.response: We agree on the ranking and I think your caveat is the right one to examine. A joint lattice-and-ion prize would need a further name from the ion-clock community, none of whom is on the shortlist, and it would dilute the clean concept that makes B031 attractive. My preference is to honour the lattice scheme specifically, acknowledging in the discussion that ion clocks are a parallel route, and to leave the ion-clock community for a later year if needed. I would be open to wording that does not exclude them in principle.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked circuit QED first and the Higgs experimental discovery (B005) second, and put B031 fifth, calling it technically spectacular and timely but raising whether ion-clock groups also deserve recognition.
responses.response: Our views differ in emphasis rather than substance, since you also call B031 original and clear. On B005 the science is beyond question, but the committee still has to decide which individuals are credited out of two collaborations of thousands, and your own note that choosing founders rather than discovery-era leaders is a judgment call shows that this is not settled. Until it is, I would be wary of ranking it above a candidate whose attribution can be stated in one sentence. On ion clocks I agree they deserve mention, and I would handle that in the discussion rather than by enlarging the prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a two-person lattice-clock prize without Lemonde, Lisdat, Takamoto, Ludlow or ion-clock groups, given the priority history of the early lattice clocks.
Whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes make a third prize on the same measurement lineage unattractive to the full committee, and whether it prefers to wait for the SI second redefinition.
Whether B016 or B028 would gather more support than B031 once the Higgs and IceCube attribution questions are discussed.
statement.conflict_note: No direct conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. A connection to report: I spent part of my doctoral period in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall's 2005 prize is part of the lineage on which Ye's work builds, so I may be seen as close to that tradition. I am also an atomic physicist at Lund working on laser spectroscopy and laser stabilisation, which overlaps methodologically with this field, though I have no documented collaboration with the candidates. My Lund collaborations (Rippe, Walther, Kinos), WACQT and Deep Light Vision relate to quantum memories and quantum technology, so they bear on B016 and B028 only indirectly; I would flag them if those candidates became central.
